subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is worth while at all times to review with care the financial position of our country in each recurring fiscal year, but it is doubly necessary that the review in these times be with especial care, fairness and thoroughness. The outcome of the struggle in which we are engaged will he decided by a preponderance of military skill on the one hand and of business organization and financial strength on the other. Which, in the ultimate, will be the controlling factor, it may be difficult to say, but our business is to see to it that whichever is supreme in the end, the one factor or the other, we are the stronger party.
The Budget deliverance this year is the most inspiring message ever given to the people of Canada by any Minister of Finance. This is the fiftieth Budget of this Dominion and it is incomparably the best of all. I say this not to boast nor to ascribe credit to the Administration in particular for these results; I say it because the results themselves are of sufficient importance and sufficiently vital to us at this time to warrant impressing them upon this House and upon the people of Canada. It is a matter of secondary concern who are chiefly to get the credit or what measures are especially to get the credit for the enviable position we are in to-day. The matter of prime importance is that we have attained the commercial strength we have and that, at this critical hour, we can face the balance of the conflict with renewed courage and vigour.
What are the results and what briefly is our position? We find ourselves in the first place in the possession of a revenue unheard of in the history of Canada, indeed undreamed of in any previous year. I realize the significance of the statement made by the leading financial critic of the Opposition, that no one could have anticipated that we would at this time be in the financial position in which we are; that %ve could have attained along commercial lines to the results that we have attained. We find ourselves in possession of a revenue of $232,000,000, or $60,000,000 in advance of our receipts in any previous year of our existence. The advance alone is more than the whole revenue of Canada fifteen years ago. Wie find ourselves in receipt of that revenue without having strangled or crippled or even impaired any line or class of industry in this country or any individual in this country, and we are able to look abroad over the land and to say * that all classes of our people from the humblest to the highest are individually and generally in a better position than they have ever been before. As against that revenue, we have an expenditure, outside of war expenditure (which, for the moment, I leave out of account), totalling $172,000,000, or practically the same as last year, included in which is the capital expenditure of $27,000,000, and an interest and pensions expenditure attributable to the war debt alone of $25,000,000. Did our system of bookkeeping assign to war expenditure all that is in reality its due, we would have an expenditure in this year of

only $147,000,000, and the surplus revenue over that total expenditure, ordinary and capital, would reach the enormous total of $85,000,000. It is argued on the part of Opposition critics-as inevitably it must be and no complaint can be found for that attitude-that even at that figure we are in excess of our expenditure of only four or five years ago. That is correct, but we are in reduction of what we have spent during the past three years.
Last year, not including interest on war debt and pensions, that expenditure of $147,000,000 on ordinary and capital account would have amounted approximately to $155,000,000. The year before it was $180,000,000, and the year before that about $183,000,000. So that within the last four years there has been a most pronounced, a most emphatic retrenchment. Going back of that again, to the times when our revenue was very much smaller, when the scope of the operations of the Dominion Government was very much more contracted than it is to-day, and when the cost of living was very much lower, we find the figure somewhat less. But what is the figure? There is no lesson to be learned, even though the result is truly told and not falsified, by taking individual patches and comparing one year with another. A great historian has said that by taking mere fragments of history you can learn nothing at all, or any lesson you like, but that if you take history as a whole you get great and salutory lessons, valuable for all time. It is the same with the history of our finance.
Looking back to the year 1909, let us say, or I will take any other year that is named, our expenditure for that year was ony 16 per cent less than the expenditure for the year we have just passed, leaving out all war accounts. Just 16 per cent difference in almost eight years of this country's history, and in the course of that time the cost of everything has increased; the scope of the operations of this Government has increased; the services we have performed for the public of Canada have multiplied. So much is this so that it would be impossible for any business concern in Canada with a like increase in its duties to show an equally small increase in its expenditure. While eight years ago we spent a sum of money on capital and ordinary expenditure of $128,200,000, only 16 per cent less than what we spent last year, our revenue in that year was only some $85,000,000. Our revenue this year is $232,000,000, or almost 300 per cent more than it was in 1909. As against almost 300 per cent of an increase in revenue
[Mr. Meiglien.l
we have an increase in expenditure, all things together outside of the war, of only 16 per cent. That is .a broad view of the situation. The figures are almost as favourable for any year you like to take back of 1911; there would be very little difference. That is a broad outlook on the way we are moving, .and on the efforts that have been made to retrench effectively in large sums. Our revenue is $232,000,000, and our expenditure $172,000,000; we have paid all our accounts on capital and ordinary expenditure-and that is what counts, it is neither the one nor the other, but the two together that counts-we have paid our interest on war debt and pensions, and have $60,000,000 to the good. Before this Government took office only in four complete years since Confederation did this country ever pay its way; two of those years were under the late Administration, and two were prior to their time. But there have been four years in which there were surpluses since this Government took office. Last year there was a surplus of about $2,000,000; another year, 1912-13, there was a surplus of $25,000,000, and the previous year a surplus of about $122,000. As I said before, previous to the taking of office by this Administration only in four complete years since Confederation did this country ever pay its way. On the other hand, those who came in Parliament at the same time as myself will remember that commencing with 1908 and going on through 1909, 1910 and part of 1911 there were very large increases in the debt. Taking the first three of those years and not the fraction of the last, this country ran behind in its expenditure over revenue to an amount exceeding $72,000,000. That was the" increase in our capital debt in three years, and part of the expenditure that we have to make to-day, which adds to our total outlay, is the interest charge on that $72,000,000 that the country ran behind in 1908, 1909 and 1910.
Now we have am increase of 16 per cent in expenditure over 1909. I will give a few reasons for that. In the first place, weTe all the conditions the same? The increase in the price we have to pay for our services would account for at least 16 per cent increase in expenditure, and we have other expenses and other services, that we did not have then. It takes a great deal more to run a railway when that railway is making $16,000,000 of revenue than it does when it is only making $8,500,000. The total revenue of the Intercolonial in 1908 was only $8,500,000, but its revenue this year is over $16,000,000, almost twice

what it was in 1908; consequently, the expenditure incumbent upon us to keep up that road is greater than it was then. But whereas in 1908 we lost $800,000 on the Intercolonial, in the year that has just gone by the Intercolonial had a surplus .of oyer $1,200,000.
I will give another reason why our expenditure is greater. There was a government that built the National Transcontinental Railway, and as a result of the necessity placed upon us by our predecessors of running that road, we are out many millions more. If they had succeeded in building another transcontinental road the expenditure, of this country would necessarily be much more than it is.
On the other hand, what is the state of the country generally with regard to trade? There is no figure that is comparable in importance to the people of this country with the figures of out export trade. A country of less than eight millions of people stripped of almost 400,000 of its young manhood by the call of war, produces and manufactures goods sufficient for the consumption of its own population, and then sells to the outside world $1,178,000,000 of surplus. War time or no war time, high prices or no high prices, there is no country in the wprld that can present figures comparable with those. Our total trade is $2,043,000,000 and of the total trade we have a balance in our favour of $314,000,000. So -that $864,500,000 is our total import and $1,178,500,000 is our total export; that is, we sold to the outside world $1,178,500,000 and bought from the outside $864,500,000 worth. The importance of the volume of our sales is very much greater than is the volumn of our purchases.
Ordinarily, large imports are not to be deplored; we cannot become a great exporter unless we import largely also. But the country that regulates and organizes its trade so as to use fully its own resources and to bring those resources to the highest value by its own industries, makes its exports greater than its imports, and so makes money out of its trade. That is the position we are in to-day; we are selling $314,000,000 more than we are buying from the outside world. This is what makes us prosperous. For we are not great carriers of trade, nor have we great investments in foreign lands. Therefore, unless we are able to make goods and sell them to the outside world we could not hope to pay our obligations. Fortunately, we have reached that position, a position of great strength
and one that must be gratifying to every citizen of Canada.

Take the exports alone -and the exports have grown more rapidly than the imports-and you find that for last year they were greater than the total exports for four years of the late Administration. These are facts that mean a great deal to Canada; they speak of the destiny of our country, and give us courage and confidence to maintain this struggle to the end.
I wish to refer briefly to certain arguments advanced by the hon. member for Red Deer. I refer to them for this reason-that I know he advances them out of regard for what he believes to be a truth, namely, that the fiscal policy of this country at this time is important from a war standpoint. It is from a war standpoint that he discusses matters in this House, and the arguments he has advanced are worthy of courteous consideration for that reason. He tells us that it would be the best thing we could do at this time to throw down our tariff wall entirely and let all goods into this country free. To follow any other course, he says, is to imitate the example of Germany and not that of Great Britain. I am as far as the hon. member from desiring to imitate the example of Germany in anything that pertains to honour, humanity, or other higher qualities of man; but I do not think it wrong to study the methods of Germany in matters of business organization, because we have not yet reached the stage at which we can ignore the results which that country has achieved by its methods. The hon. gentleman pointed out that Germany, at the opening of the war, had thrown down the barriers and had removed tariff restrictions from certain goods, such as bread-stuffs, fats, and other foods. Well, if we were to do that also we should be following Germany's example. But I cannot understand the attitude of mind that would cite this as being a denial of the protective system by Germany in time of war. What is the object of that protective system? It is to give German -producers a better hold upon the German market. After the war broke out and the British navy was on the water, there was not much necessity to use the tariff to keep the home market for the German producer-the British navy saw to it that there was not much competition from outside. Consequently, there was no longer reason for a tariff on foodstuffs-quite the contrary. The hon. gentleman said: The ship of free trade in Great Britain stood the
[Mr. Melghen.l
storm, the ship of free trade is the ship that I go in; free trade has been maintained by Great Britain in this struggle. It is nothing but a misnomer to say that Great Britain is a free trade country. It levies duties greater in amount than those levied in Canada; last year Great Britain collected $350,000,000 in tariff duties. We collected only $134,000,000. And, instead of diminishing or removing tariff duties because of the war, they have put on new duties and increased old ones. And these increases of duty are not on luxuries only, but on necessities also. They have resorted to the tariff to raise revenues for this war, and in doing so they have added to the protective effect of that tariff. Let me give you a few of the articles upon which they have increased their duties. They have diminished duties, as far as I can find, on nothing whatsoever.

It is not freedom for the people within the country to trade with eaoh other just as they individually please or vfith the outside world as they like. We are not fighting for protection or freedom of trade or freedom in that sense at all; we are fighting for the freedom of our nation and lof every other nation to decide for free trade or protection or to decide for anything else that the democracy of that country demands. We are fighting for the freedom of our nation as a nation, and freedom not only for ourselves, but for every country, within its own domain, to decide upon its own course as it wishes, undisturbed and unprovoked by aggression from without. Freedom of trade is no more what we are fighting for {ban is the protective system. We are fighting for the right, once and for all, to decide which we will have, free trade, protection, or anything else that we may desire.
It is inevitable in Canada, where we have a tremendous geographical extent, where we have a wide diversity of interests, and a wide diversity of activities, and where that diversity is chiefly marked by a long stretch of country that separates the one portion from the other, where we have in one-half of the Dominion a very large, preponderant agricultural community producing a share of the raw material of the world, the foodstuffs of the world, and where we have in the other half of the Dominion, with a much larger proportion of population, a more highly commercialized people, a manufacturing population on a very considerable scale, a population engaged in many industries and many activities and manufacturing to a larger extent than is possible in our western country-it is inevitable, in such a country as we have here, that the protective tariff which we maintain must he only a moderate protective tariff, a tariff that has regard to the preponderant views of tooth sections of this country. It cannot have sole regard to any preponderance of sentiment in the East, nor can it have sole regard to any preponderant sentiment in the West. Both must be most carefully considered with a view to that unity which is essential if a nation is to prosper and which at this time is doubly essential, is vital to our success. It is an inevitable and indisputable fact that the prevailing sentiment west of the Great Lakes, and particularly in the three grain-

producing prairie provinces, favours a lower tariff than does the prevailing sentiment in eastern Canada. That is not only on admitted truth, tout it is a truth that is born of and imbedded in our geography, that is born of and imbedded in the conditions of our national life. The people in those three provinces are the great producers of our grain. They are not a manufacturing people. Consequently they do not get as immediate or as direct results from the maintenance of a protective tariff as do the people in the other portions of Canada. One cannot argue from that that they should not in that country have regard to the whole interests of Canada and not merely to those of the three provinces. Nor can it be argued that the sentiment of western Canada pan he ignored by the citizens of this eastern country, or toy the Parliament or Government of this Dominion in the framing of its fiscal policy.

The war has progressed for many, many months and the activities of German submarines and many other activities have had the result of diminishing to a very great degree the volume of British shipping.
One result of that is that it has been impossible for Great Britain to permit the free importation of goods on the same scale as before. The British Commission purchasing in Canada-and no doubt this is true in the United States as well-is the only purchaser for export, for nobody else can get space in ships. In our western country there was a large proportion of the wheat that could not reach any of these higher grades, a larger proportion indeed, by reason of the conditions described by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff), than usually has prevailed. There was no export price, because there was no export market. When the duty was taken off, on the 16th of April, the Minneapolis price on 1, 2, and 3 Northern fell at once to the export level, that-

When the bell rang this morning there was a moment of silence, then a small voice offered to sell wheat at $2.29, at $2.28g, and at $2.28|. No response was made and the voice shut up. Now, as to the alleged point that this Order in Council will die at the termination of the war and that consequently it would he wise now to legislate as to what should he done afterwards, I say, first, that if ever an amendment 'bore on its face the earmarks of political chicanery it is this amendment. It is an attempt to raise a douht in the minds of western Canadians; it is an attempt to raise a douht in the minds of the officials of the United States of America-although it has failed in that object-as to whether or not this Act is not of some peculiar temporary character on which we should not rely. Nobody ever thought of such a doubt before. I never heard it even whispered. The War Measures Act gives to the Government of Canada power to enact Orders and regulations having regard to a number of subjects recited in the Act, and one, if not more than one, of those classes of subjects clearly embraces the action we took. That legislation having been passed, the Government was then in a position to do what otherwise only Parliament could do, enact and enforce orders, regulations and laws binding upon the people of this country. We so enact, and what we do is to enact a law just as if it had been done by this Parliament. It is done by the Government under the authority of this Parliament, which means that it is done by this Parliament.
Just as if it were in the Act itself.	*
I am glad that I have convinced a legal member of the Opposition.
It does not need any convincing; it is absolutely clear on its face.

Consequently it takes effect just as if we legislated in Parliament that these duties were removed and it has just the same effect as if this Parliament, by specific enactment, had removed the duty. It is argued by the hon. member for Halifax that at the end of the war the Order in Council lapses and that consequently the duties that were removed under the Order in Council must be restored, or, rather, would be automatically restored. I hardly know how to put the absurdity of that position in clearer form than I put it to the hon. member while he was speaking, that once we legislate by Order in Council under an Act that gives us power 
to legislate, that is legislation, and it has the same effect, the same permanence and the same finality that any other legislation has. All legislation may be amended, may be repealed. This, like all other legislation, may be amended or repealed. It has the same permanence and the same finality as any legislation passed by this House. What is done by Order in Council while the War Measures Act is alive is legislation and remains legislation just the same as any legislation passed by this House.
If it were different, what would be the result? Under the War Measures Act-to take the example that I took before-we by Order in Council appropriated to this country the title to the Eoss rifle factory in Quebec. We have enacted other Acts of a similar character. If the legislation lapses with this Parliament and the effect of what we do must be reversed, what will be the result in the case I have mentioned? In March of this year we declared that the title of Sir Charles Eoss to that factory ceased to be his and became ours. If the hon. member for Halifax is correct, when the war is over that title ceases to be ours and goes back to Sir Charles Eoss, although we have paid for it, although he has the money, although he may be dead or may have spent the money. This is utterly absurd and clearly shows that there cannot be the faintest reason or ground for the contention that the hon. gentleman advances.
I am afraid the hon. gentleman has not read the War Measures Act.

Here is an amendment to a motion to go into Committee of Ways and Means. It calls upon us to pass a vote of adulation on hon. gentlemen opposite, tp pass a reflection on this House and on the law officers of the 'Crown, and to do so for no purpose in the wprld except that of meeting the political exigencies of hoft. gentlemen opposite. What they are sorry for is that this grievance in which they have revelled for so many years is now removed. They want to keep alive the agitation which has been their chief hppo in western Canada. They are anxious to stir up and keep white the embers of a controversy without which there is not very much light for them on the horizon. Now that that controversy is removed and removed with such permanence as it is within the power of this Parliament to effect they are not satisfied; they want to dp something which will retain to them some of the advantages they hoped to gain by that agitation all through these years. That is the purpose of this amendment. The Deputy Minister of Justice says that the legislation has the same permanence as any legislation ever passed by this Parliament. We must be governed in matters of law by the opinion of the law officers of this Government; otherwise we are untrue to our trust. The amendment of the hon. member for Assiniboia, boiled down, is nothing more or less than this: " Whereas I, John G. Turriff and somebody else whose name I will not give, should be accepted on matters of law by the Parliament of Canada in preference to the responsible law officers of the Crown; therefore be it resolved that we do over again something that is already done, with all the finality and permanence that is in the power of Parliament to do it." That is the amendment which the hon. member for Assiniboia solemnly asks us to pass.

Would it not be possible for this Government to repeal that Order in Council by another Order in Council? And, if that is -so, how can the hon. gentleman say that the Order in Council has the same weight and permanency as though it were an Aot pf Parliament?

Certainly it is in our
power to repeal it, and if we pass this resolution and bring in a statute we could also repeal the statute. They are both on the same ground exactly.
No.

The authority under which we may remove duties as a war measure is the very same authority under which we may impose duties as a war measure. Both aTe exactly on the same basis; consequently, if we pass the amendment and introduce the legislation that it calls for, that legislation would be temporary in the same sense that this is temporary and it would be permanent in the same sense that this is permanent.
That is, if your majority did not change its mind.
Exactly so; the hon. member for Red Deer has the point exactly.
But you could not do it behind the backs of the representatives of the people.

Yes, the power would undoubtedly exist. I have to thank the House for the patience with which my altogether too much prolonged discourse has been received. I refer again to the matter of greatest moment in this Budget. The motion of my hon. friend is not the matter of greatest moment; it was my duty to refer to it fully and at length because I, in part, represent western Canada in the Administration. But the outstanding feature is the successful commercial course that this country has pursued, the strong position that it occupies, the course that we have taken in bringing business to Canada and in retaining business here by our policies. And in the bringing of some of that business to Canada no one deserves more credit than the ex-Minister of Militia himself. The outstanding feature is that by the business we are doing, the goods we are producing, we are able to sustain our country through this struggle and can sustain it to the end. That is the gratifying element of this Budget. It is important that no one should allow any mere secondary feature or any amendment, whatever be its design, to draw our attention from this great achievement, and it is important that the people of Canada, reviewing the statement for the year, take from it that renewed inspiration, courage and confidence which the awful tasks confronting us require, and which an enlightened study of our deeds already done can scarcely fail to command.

Mr. Speaker, I am not sure as to whether my sympathies ought to 'be extended more to the gentlemen who are sitting behind the Government benches than to my hon. friend the Solicitor Generali during the course of his speech this afternoon. It is evident that the hon. gentleman's efforts were directed entirely to justifying the conduct of the Government in the eyes of their supporters. There could be no other reason for his long speech, first in condemnation, and, secondly, in justification of this Order in Council. The hon. gentleman devoted a good deal of his time to showing that the Government had been right in resisting the demands of the Liberal party and of the people of the West that wheat and wheat products should be placed upon the free list. He gave very strong reasons, and I think anyone reading that portion of his speech in Hansard would come to the conclusion that there would be a very great danger to-morrow, or within a week, or within a month, if the hon. gentleman had his way in the Cabinet of having this Order in Council repealed, because, as I have said, the hon. gentleman has told us that he has not changed his mind, and that he believes the refusal of the Government in the past to place wheat and wheat products upon the free list was entirely in the best interest of the country and in accordance with the great principles of the national policy. But, Sir, the hon. gentleman was obliged, of course, to give some reasons why the Government had acted. The extraordinary thing which the hon. gentleman has done is that at last he seems to have been driven by the peculiar workings of his own mind to justify this Order in Council on the ground that it has given to the small millers in Canada a market for their flour in the United States.
I said that?

Yes, because, as I understood him to say, it gives them the opportunity to dispose of their finished product. The hon. gentleman says that it is much more important for the people to have a market for their finished product than for their raw material, and that on that ground the Order in Council may be supported.
I intend to deal with the points which my hon. friend has made with regard to this Order in Council, to refer to the amendment, and to show that instead of being the very horrible thing that my hon. friend thinks it is, it is an amendment which ought to commend itself to all the members of this House. Before doing this, however, I should like to refer very briefly to the remarks which my hon. friend made with reference to the state of the trade of the country. That was the subject of my hon. friend's remarks in the earlier part of his discourse, and after the lugubrious performance which he had given us with respect to free wheat, he returned to this cheerful trade condition in order, I suppose, to bring his supporters out of the slough of despond into which he had driven them by his reference to the free wheat policy. The hon. gentleman referred to the fact that the trade of Canada-and in this respect he followed the Minister of Finance -had reached, during the past fiscal year, the enormous sum of upwards of $2,000,000,000. He spoke of this, as did the Minister of Finance, as being a most cheering condition of affairs. Think of it, said my hon. friend, that in a very few years the export and import trade of Canada had risen from $600,000,000 to upwards of $2,000,000,000. I almost wondered why my hon. friend did not come down with a resolution thanking the Kaiser for the magnificent prosperity which he had brought to Canada, because it is the Kaiser who is responsible for it all; it is not the Minister of Finance nor the Solicitor General; it is not the Government of this country; it is not the ordinary business development or the ordinary prosperity of the people of Canada; it is by reason of the bringing about of this bloody war by the Kaiser and his Government. Surely, when we are considering as to whether Canada is in a prosperous condition or not, we ought to have regard to the normal condition of affairs; we ought to consider whether the manufactures of Canada are developing in such a way as to bring permanent prosperity to the people of this country; we ought to consider whether the country is being developed by new settlers who are coming in and cultivating our vacant land. If that were the condition of affairs, we might rejoice at it. But instead of rejoicing at the fact that this condition of affairs exists to-day, the people of Canada ought to have a feeling of sadness because it is owing to these terrible war

Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) tells us that this granting of free wheat is a very different proposition from the reciprocity arrangement. It is different only in degree. Suppose that there was no statute of the United States permitting the free entry of wheat into that country on our making it free in this country, and suppose that the Minister of Finance, impressed toy the reasons that induced this Government to pass the Order in Council in favour of free wheat, had gone to Washington to secure for Canada that benefit; discussing the matter with the Secretary of State of the United States he would say: we do not wish to arrange for the free admission of a large number of articles, but we would like to make an arrangement for free wheat, wheat flour, and semolina, but it must be understood that each country is to be absolutely free to repeal this legislation whenever it thinks it in the interest of its own people. Had this been done, in what respect would it have been different from that which has been done to-day? When these gentlemen were confronted with this problem did they draw up an Order in Council having no regard to what the United States had done? Not at all. They consulted the statutes of the United States and .adopted the very wording of their statute on this subject. They did not even use words broad enough to confer upon the eastern farmer the boon of free bran and shorts from the United States with which to feed his cattle. They did not use t'he words they might have used, " wheat and wheat products," but they used the words " wheat, wheat flour, and semolina," the very words used in the statute of the United States.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Pugsley) interrupted me to say that the reciprocity agreement made these products free, but I find that it provided a duty of $2.45 a ton on bran. Will the hon. gentleman explain why t'he Government of which he was a member did not give the farmers at that time the " boon " of which he speaks?
The hon. gentleman may be correct as to its not being free, but at all events the arrangement made a great reduction.

" boon " of free bran given?

There is another question I would like to ask: Why did not this 'Government wait until Parliament opened before it passed this Order in Council? Here is the inauguration of a policy of enormous importance affecting the trade between these tw.o countries. It applies to the most important product of Canada. It is the chief natural product of the two countries and here it is proposed to take advantage of the reciprocal provision-you cannot call it anything else- in the statutes of the United States under which this great product will pass freely between the two countries. This Government, and the party which stands behind it, had, in 1911, told the people of Canada that our great railway systems had been built east and west for the purpose of carry, ing trade east and west instead of north and south. They had taken the ground that it would bring down the very keystone of the National Policy if this should be adopted. They had taken that ground when, in 1911 it was proposed to make an arrangement with the United States, not an arrangement binding either country for all time but an arrangement which, just like this statutory arrangement could have been repealed at the will of the Parliament or Congress at any time, as clearly appears from the correspondence which took place between the Hon. Mr. Fielding and Secretary Knox. Now, they are proposing to reverse the policy for which they had asked

the approval of the people of Canada. Did they wait until the representatives of the people had gathered in this Parliament from the Western shores of Canada, from the East, from the great provinces of Ontario and Quebec and from other sections of Canada? Did they await to consult Parliament's opinion? Did they even wait to consult their own supporters? No, Sir, instead of doing that they gave them no opportunity of presenting their views, and the views of the people who sent them to this Parliament, but on the 16th April, three days before Parliament re-assembled, behind the backs of the people's representatives, they passed this Order in Council.

Is my bon. friend
aware that the hon. member for Assiniboia, a year ago, complained that we had not done this very thing by Order in Council?

not in session.

We were demanding that this should be done in the interest of the people, of the country and gentlemen on the other side of the House were saying that it was utterly indefensible to do it, that it was contrary to the policy which the people had sustained in 1911, that it would be contrary tp the pledge they had made to the people of Canada upon which they secured their support and upon which they relied to get into this Parliament as their representatives that they should dp anything of the kind. Why did they not consult their friends? It was because they knew that they would not be likely to support them in caucus. But they know also that when they get a measure passed in Council so that they are committed to it they can rely upon their friends not going back upon them and sustaining them even though it is with many heartburnings. ^r- PUGSLEY: Yes, and it was submitted to, and had to meet with the approval of Parliament before becoming law. By the terms of the letters which passed between the two negotiators it was expressly stated that it should be submitted .both to the Parliament of this country and to the Congress 554
of the United States before it should go into effect. Our Government would, not have so defied public opinion as to enter into am arrangement of that kind, except it was subject to the approval of Parliament.
Was there any great urgency? Can you think of any urgency that there was? It was the 16th of April. The wheat had practically all passed out of the 1 ands of the farmers in the West. We know that in the West the farmer threshes his grain in November. He gets it to the elevator and markets it just as speedily as he can. There are very few farmers, I venture to say-my hon. friends from the West will correct me if I am wrong-who hold any large quantity of grain in their hands after the first of February, or the first of March, subsequent to the year in which it is har->
vested. All the elevators are filled with grain. It is largely in the hands of the speculator. Can any one suggest any great object In passing that Order in Council on the 16th of April when Parliament was reassembling on the 19th of April and when their supporters in .Parliament should have been consulted before taking that step?
And the Budget speech had not been delivered.

The Budget speech had not been delivered. I venture to say that the people will want to know the reason for this hurried action. I would not charge that it was intended to put money into the hands of these sepeculators for the reason that it would raise the price of wheat and would make a product which they had bought from the farmers at from 75 cents to $1.25 a bushel very largely worth from $2.25 to $2.40 a bushel. I would not suggest anything of the kind. What, then, was the reason for it? Why not wait until Parliament and the people's representatives could be taken into the confidence of hon. gentlemen? Parliament is the great council room of the nation. It is the place where the people, through their representatives, ought to be informed as to these questions and consulted in regard to actions of this nature which the Governrhent propose to take. But, no Sir, they passed it through without first consulting their own supporters.
Now, my hon. friend the Solicitor General makes the statement that the Deputy Minister of Justice says that this Order in Council has the effect of legislation. I am glad that my hon. friend and I are in

accord as to the effect of the Order in Council. The Order in Council has exactly the same force and effect as if it had been made part of the statute. There is no doubt about that. That is the way that it is construed always.
It has the force of any statute.	%
It has the force of any statute on which it is based.
Of any statute.

Of any statute on which it is based. It is like the rules made under: a judicature Act. These Orders |n Council are not unknown at all, they are not unusual and they are not unique in character. Take a statute providing for a judicature Act; in England and wherever a judicature act has been passed; the Legislature has given to the Supreme Court the power to make rules which have the force of the statute just the same as if they were enacted in the judicature Act itself. So, in regard to boards of health; every board of health act provides that the provincial board of health may make rules and regulations which have the force of law just as if they were enacted by statute. In England and in this country you will find numbers of statutes which are passed giving to certain bodies, sometimes to the Governor in Council, sometimes to another public body, power to make orders or rules and regulations which are to have the force of law. Now, Sir, these rules and these orders are what are known as subordinate legislation. But, Sir, they must depend for their validity and their endurance must depend upon the basic Statute upon which they are founded and for the carrying out of which these different parties are given power to make such orders. Take the case of a Board of Health which is created and power given to it to make regulations which are to have the force of law just as if they were enacted in the Statute creating the Board of Health. But that Board of Health is to last three years, the Act creating it is to come to an end in three years. Would it be argued that when the Board of Health goes out of existence as the result of the expiry of the temporary Statute that the regulations would still stand and that they could still be enforced?
The effect of them would stand.
Not at all.

Anything done under
them would stand.

There are two kinds of Statutes known to the law, as my hon. friend knows. One of them is what is known as a perpetual Statute and the other a temporary Statute or Act. A perpetual Act is one to which there is no limitation. While it can be repealed at any time by Act of Parliament, it is known as a perpetual Act. You will find that distinction in all text books. Now this War Measures Act happens to be a temporary Act. My hon. friend has not called attention to that. He has spoken of this as if it were like any other Statute; it is called the War Measures Act but he treats it as though it were like any other Act. Some parts of it are perpetual but some parts and the most vital are temporary and are to expire at the termination of the war.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MR. J. H. BURNHAM.
speechtext:
I wish to rise to a
question of privilege. On Thursday evening, the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Niclcle), as appears by Hansard, spoke regarding my remarks on venereal diseases.
I wish to say that my reference was to the question of venereal diseases and the war at large, and not to aiiy specific army, as a perusal of the reporter's notes will show.
I have re-read the reporter's notes and find no instance of the use of the word " Canadian " by me in that connection, but simply a reference to Canada's possibly being in danger after the war, meaning, of course, to refer to immigration, although I did not use the word " immigration."

Consideration of the proposed motion of Sir Thomas White (Minister of Finance) for the Committee of Ways and Means, and of the amendment of Mr. Turriff thereto, resumed.
Hon. Mr. PUGSLEY i(resuming):	Before the House rose at six o'clock, I was proceeding to argue that this Order in Council was of a temporary character. It is in the nature of temporary war legislation, and the Solicitor General and myself both agreed-in fact, he was rather pleased, as he thought, to convince me of his assertion, but I did not require any convincing because it was absolutely clear law that any subordinate legislation which any body, whether the Governor in Council or a' Board of Health, or any similar body has the power to make, has the same effect as if it had been enacted by Statute.
What I said was "in any statute."

Does not my hon. friend see that Section 7 simply provides the means for paying for the factory? It does not affect the point at all. If what my hon. friend says is correct, the title would revert back to the Ross Rifle Company after the war. Section 7 makes no provision of that kind whatever.
Anything that has been completed while the temporary Act is in force is carried to a conclusion and becomes effective.
This is completed.

Parliament may have taken the property, but not have paid for it before the end of the war, and to meet such a case, Parliament provides the means of paying for the property even after the war has come to an end; section 7 was passed for that purpose. But, as I have said, section 6, under which this Order in Council was passed, is temporary in its character, and ends immediately on the conclusion of the war. It has very often happened that a question has arisen as to the effect of a temporary Act, and there is one important case referred to in a very valuable book entitled Craie's Statute Law, which is based upon Hardeastle, an authority of the very greatest merit. In this text book a

case will be found where a question arose as to whether a temporary Act had the effect of repealing a franchise under which certain tolls were collected, or whether it merely suspended the operation of the franchise. The court held that it would depend upon what was the apparent intention as expressed by the Act of Parliament. In one case it was provided that the temporary Act should continue for a certain period of time and until the close of the then next session of Parliament, and the court was convinced that the intention of Parliament in passing the temporary Act was that, at its expiration application should be made to Parliament to deal with the matter. The court held that as the intention was that application should be made to Parliament, the franchise was repealed. It is always a question, no matter whether the Act deals with regulations, tolls or anything else provided for by another. Act, whether the latter Act is simply suspended in its operations, or repealed.
There is not a line or a word in this statute from which it could be inferred that Parliament had any intention of continuing sections 6, 10, 11, and 13 or anything done under these sections one day beyond the termination of the war. If that be so, this subordinate legislation, this Order in Council, must end with the basic legislation upon which it is founded. It certainly could not have been intended by Parliament to give a subordinate body, which is what the Governor in Council is, greater power than that which is exercised by Parliament itself. Parliament in this legislation is dealing with temporary matters, it is enacting that which it is desirable to enact because of the exigencies of war. Had the provisions of this Order in Council been enacted directly by Parliament as part, of section 6, instead of as subordinate legislation by Order in Council under that section, it would have come to an end with the war. The Solicitor General admitted that-he was obliged to do so. As the authorities show that subordinate legislation is to be construed as if it were contained in the basic Act itself, and as this section of the statute comes to an end with the war, the Order in Council based upon it cannot have a longer life. On this point I will refer to this same authority, Craies. At page 262 he gives examples of what in England are called "statutory rules"-subordinate legislation having the force of law. He says:
The most salient examples or statutory rules are the Rules of the Supreme Court (infMr. Pugsley.J
eluding' the Crown Office Rules), the County Court Rules, the Summary" Jurisdiction Rules, the Regulations to Prevent Collisions at Sea, and many, if not most, Orders in Council.
There is nothing sacred about an Order in Council any mpre than about a regulation made by any other authority given power by statute to make it. Craies further says:
Under certain statutes it is directed-
(1)	That Orders in Council, etc., made under the statute are to have the same effect as if enacted therein; or
(2)	That rules when made are to lie on the tables of both Houses of Parliament for a certain time; or
(3)	That the validity of the order, etc., shall not be judicially questioned.
The case of Institute of Patent Agents, v. Lockwood suggests that in the first of these cases "the proper canon of construction is to read the original Act and the subordinate legislation together as if they were one Act and were to be construed together ;'* and it is submitted that the same rule applies to cases (2) and (3).
Thus, when a statute gives authority to any body or person, whether the Governor in Council, or a board of health, or a court, any order made under that statute is to be constructed with the statute on which it is founded, and when, by effluxion of time, the statute becomes of no effect, the order made in pursuance of it and based upon it also comes to an end. That is subject always to this consideration-that if Parliament has clearly shown an intention that the subordinate legislation is to continue after the expiration of the statute, the courts will give effect to it. In cases where a temporary Act suspends the operation of a franchise or the levying of tolls, then, when the temporary Act expires, the statute whose operation was by it suspended ipso facto comes into force again, just as before the temporary Act was passed.
That nothing can be done under a temporary Act after it expires has been established in a number of cases. There is one rather interesting case to be found in Craies at page 338. Mr. O'Connell was charged with an offence under a temporary Act. When brought to trial he pleaded guilty. But he was not punished, and many thought that this was because of political pressure having been brought to bear. But when inquiry was made it was found that, though he had been tried and had pleaded guilty during the continuance of the temporary Act, afterwards that temporary Act had expired before sentence and there was thus no power to sentence him.
I have spoken of instances in which Parliament has clearly made provision that

If the Government advance a certain opinion they are certainly denying the contrary but when the hon. gentleman finds a certain section demonstrating that this Government can do a certain thing would he interpret it as being intended to prevent them from doing that thing?
Put it on the Statute Books so that there would he no mistake.

If I were in power I would say absolutely that I would feel bound to take the position that this is a temporary Act, and that the customs duties would nt its termination come into force. The temporary Act expires when the war terminates and the customs duties again become operative. The Deputy Minister of Justice says that the order has the effect of ^legislation-we all admit that-of subordinate legislation-and then he says that these duties are removed by this temporary Act, which, of course, is entirely consistent with the position I take that they are temporarily removed, and that they can only come into operation again by the authority of. Parliament. And he says that wheat, wheat flour and semolina will remain free unless fresh duties be imposed by or under the authority of Parliament.
Read the whole of the last sentence, please.

I will read it.
Therefore, I am of opinion that the Order in Council became effective as from its date permanently to remove the duty imposed by the present customs tariff on wheat, wheat flour and semolina and that these products accordingly become free of customs duty, and will remain free unless fresh duties be imposed by or under the authority of Parliament.
What . does ''perman-nently" mean?

Upon reading it again I am inclined to think that Mr. Newcombe

must mean permanently. The idea I had before was that it was until the duties were reimposed under the authority of Parliament, but the word "permanently" would rather indicate that Mr. Nevvcombe's opinion is that it is permanent, and I should be disposed to leave it at that.
Oh, oh.

It is the pride of members of the legal profession that they admit at once when they make an error, and I gladly admit that I misinterpreted Mr. Neweombe. But, while I have great respect for Mr. Newcombe's opinion, I am inclined to think that there has been a failure to call his attention to the authority of Hardcastle and Craies, because these authorities are absolutely clear that when an Act temporary in its character prevents the collection of duties and tolls and the exercise of franchises, that Act, at the end of the time when it is declared that it shall be in operation, shall cease to be in force, and, ipso facto, the ancient franchise will be restored and1 the tolls or duties provided by statute will go into force again unless there is an expression of a clear intention on the part of Parliament to the contrary. '
Supposing I should be in error as to this, then there is the other fact which cannot by any possibility be gotten over, that the Governor in Council is expressly given by this statute the power to revoke this order at any time during the war. They cannot do it afterwards because the authority ends with the war. Under section 6 they have authority to revoke it at any time during the war. These are the words contained in section 6, sub-section 2, the. statute under which this order is passed, and they are as clear as language can be:
All orders and regulations made under this section shall have the force of law and shall he enforced in such manner and hy such courts, officers and authorities, as the Governor in Council niay prescribe, and may he varied, extended or revoked hy any subsequent order or regulation. *
There is the clear authority given by section 6 of this statute, the same statute which, during the war, gives the power to make an order and to enforce it during the war and also the power to revoke it. There is no question about that. That shows that the order is temporary in its character. It shows that if the Government should desire to do so, they might, behind the back of the public and behind the backs of members of this 'Parliament, in secret
fMr. Pugsley.]
session, in council, at any time, revoke this order and restore the duties on wheat, wheat flour and semolina under the Customs Act.
So that whether its temporary character is ensured Iby the fact that that Act is temporary and wi'll expire at the termination of the war, or whether it is temporary in its character because, without reference to Parliament, the Governor in Council has the power, to-morrow or at any time it pleases to do so, to revoke this Order and to place these products again under a duty, the argument which is made by the gentleman who moved the amendment and those who support it from this side of the House in favour of placing these products on the free list by Act of Parliament and so doing away with its temporary character, takes on the greatest possible force. Gan anybody dispute that? And if any one were to pay attention to the argument of the 'Solicitor General to-day I should say there would he the greatest possible danger, if that hon. gentleman can carry weight with Council, that the Order may be revoked very soon, and particularly in view of the fact that we had not a full Cabinet Council in Canada when the Order was passed. The Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), another important minister representing a Manitoba constituency, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers), and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) were all absent; indeed, I think even the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) was away at the time; so that 'four very important members of the Cabinet were absent. Now, what may happen a little later on, when, perhaps, a different view may prevail? The Solicitor General, if any weight is to be given to his argument to-day, has endeavoured to convince this House and this country that he and his colleagues were right in the view which they took a year ago, when they stood up in this House and voted against free wheat. His argument is along these lines, and I am sorry to say that his argument places the Solicitor General and this Government in the rather unenviable position of bringing down an Order in Council which they do not believe will be in the public interest, if we may credit what they say. Because what is the fact, and what does the Solicitor General say when you boil it down? He says, as a 'last reason why this Order should have been passed, that while he thinks that a majority of the whole people of Canada would be against it, yet out in the West, through the act of these dreadful Grits, through their repeated agitation,

they have really convinced the people out there that free wheat would be in the interest of the country; the majority of the people of Canada do not believe that, but the people in the West, these poor easily misguided farmers, have been persuaded by Grit 'speakers on the platform and in this House, and it is not desirable, particularly when an election is at hand, to have any large section of the people dissatisfied.
Election?
Yes, that is the effect of what the hon. gentleman says.
What election?
Alberta and Saskatchewan.

What does it mean? It means that upon a great question, a question of the trade relations between these two great countries involving the greatest natural products of both countries, upon a great question upon which the Conservative party came into power in 1911, upon which they asked the people to give them their support and their confidence, and upon which they succeeded in getting a majority of the representatives of the people, the hon. gentleman in effect says: Notwithstanding all that, notwithstanding our position at that time and ever since upon the trade question, notwithstanding that we have asked our followers to stand up in this House and vote down resolutions of a similar character in the past, and although I thought then we were right and I think still we were right, yet for fear that we shall lose some Conservative support out in western Canada, we are going to swallow our principles and give to these dreadful Grits what they have been asking for.
It hurts but we are going to do it.

I should like to read this Order in Council. I think it is the most unique document ever presented to Parliament, particularly coming from a Government that thinks it was unwise to pass it, particularly coming from a Government whose Solicitor General has eagerly searched the newspapers from day to day in order to present to this Parliament evidence that it was unwise to pass it, that instead of having the effect of increasing the price of wheat it has' really lowered the price of wheat.
No I did not, not at all.

Let me read it Mr. Speaker:
At the Government House, Ottawa, Monday, the 16th day of April, 1917. Present:	His
Excellency the Governor General in Council.
Whereas the Minister of Finance reports that certain conditions arising out of the war seriously affect prices obtainable in Canada for wheat, especially of the lower grades-
And, Sir, bear in mind that that was passed at a time when Canadian wheat was quoted at $2.20 per bushel. On the 16th day of April, the very day when this Order in Council was passed, wheat was quoted ,at more than $2.20, and yet the minister says:-
Whereas the Minister of Finance reports that certain conditions arising out of the war seriously effect prices obtainable in. Canada for wheat, especially of the lower grades

Now, you see, that is rather put on the ground that it is owing to the low prices of wheat that they have been brought to the serious consideration of the passing of this Order. Wheat was only 2.29i when this Order was passed. Why, what sympathetic consideration the Minister of Finance must have for the farmers of Canada when he will violate every principle which has animated him for the last five years on this trade question, when he recognizes that he got into this Parliament upon the *cry of "No truck or trade with the Yankees." How tremendously he must have been overwhelmed by the low price of wheat, $2.29 a bushel, when he sat down to write this recommendation to Council. He says:
Whereas in normal times there exists a good commercial export demand for milling purposes from Great Britain and the Continent for wheat of all grades

Now Sir, what 'are meant by normal times? They would he times of peace, would they not? And what is the highest price of wheat in times of peace? Not one dollar a bushel and in normal 9 p.m. times the minister would do nothing for the farmers, when the farmers were getting only one dollar a. bushel.
Less.

Less than a dollar a
bushel. In 1915 it was only ninety cents a bushel.
Whereas in normal times there exists a good commercial export demand for milling purposes from Great Britain and the Continent for wheat of all grades

\

There was no necessity of doing anything for the farmer when wheat was at the price it was in normal times, ninety cents per bushel.
And whereas this demand has for some time past almost entirely ceased on account of shortage of ocean shipping due to submarine warfare, practically all available tonnage being required to transport grain of the higher grades and flour made therefrom, purchased in [DOT] Canada and the United States by the British and Allied Governments for their respective needs.
One would suppose that, getting as they do a price 100 per cent more than they ever got before or even dreamed of getting in normal times, the farmers would not have found it a very great hardship to pay the duty upon the lower grades of wheat going into the United States. Even then they would not do too badly as compared with their condition in normal times, when their appeals never touched the hearts of members of this Government. This order proceeds:
And whereas in consequence of this condition wheat is being exported to the United' States market for sale there, notwithstanding the customs duty payable thereon under the provisions of the United States tariff.
So it is in consequence- of the fact that the farmers are getting $2.29 a bushel for 'their high grade wheat and that they are sending their lower grade wheat to the United States and paying duty thereon, that the attention of the Minister of Finance is directed to this most important and most disturbing question. So they would have us believe, by this beautiful Order in Council.
Disorder in Council.

They must get this thing through quickly before Parliament reassembles, and they make inquiries from the Grain Commissioners. The order recites:
And whereas from inquiries recently made from the Board of Grain Commissioners for Canada and other authentic sources the Minister of Finance is satisfied' that the prices now prevailing in Canada for wheat, particularly of the lower grades, are, owing to the cause above mentioned, much lower than the prices obtained therefor in the United States.
No.
" Much lower than the prices obtained therefor in the United States."
Who admits that?

The farmers are getting, as I said before, $2.29 for wheat of the

higher grade, and they are selling large quantities in the United States, paying duty of 10 cents a bushel. Then the order proceeds:
In fact, there are strong grounds for the belief that advantage is being taken of the situation to maintain prices of the said grades at figures lower than are warranted by general market conditions, and from information at hand it appears that there still remains a large amount of last year's Canadian crop unmarketed.
And whereas it is desirable at a time when a special appeal Is being made for increased agricultural production to supply grain and foodstuffs to Great Britain and her Allies, which now include the United States of America, that the Canadian farmer should feel that he will obtain the best market prices obtainable for product of his industry.
But the Government having waited until April 16, after the cropping season is opened, the farmer will not be able to avail himself of this order so as to enlarge his crop during the present year.- If my information is correct, the people whose unfortunate financial condition appeals to the Minister of Finance and his colleagues are the speculators who months ago bought up the wheat from the farmers and have it stored in the elevators all the way from Calgary to Montreal and Quebec. The order proceeds :
And whereas, the Minister of Finance is of the opinion that it is in the circumstances advisable that such action should he taken which would give to Canadian wheat free access to the markets of the United States-*
Now the minister is beginning to talk upon broad principles.
He was against that.
One year ago.
That is when he began to be again-st it.

How pitiable it is that when we come near the time that we have to face the electors, pur principles are scattered to the dust. " In the circumstances." In what circumstances? In the circumstances that Western wheat to-day is 100 per cent higher than it has ever been in the history of the country. (Reading):
It is in the circumstance? advisable that such action should be taken which will give to Canadian wheat free access to the markets of the United States in lieu of the .commercial markets in Great Britain and on the European continent.
In lieu of them! A man is sometimes appointed to a position in lieu of somebody that is dead. The minister is now going to

seek the American market in lieu of the European market. He goes on:
In lieu of the commercial markets in Great Britain and on the European continent, forjn-eily available under the conditions then existing, and, with this object in view, he directs the attention of His Excellency to certain provisions of the Customs Tariff of the United States.
Have you not, Sir, often heard the Prime Minister and other members of the Government, speaking in this House of the reciprocal statutory arrangement which was to be made under the negotiations between Mr. Fielding and the Secretary of State of the United States, assert in tones of thunder that we should legislate in the interests of Canada independently of what the Congress of the United States might do in the way of legislation? And yet the Finance Minister calls the attention of His Excellency to certain provisions of the United States tariff. He goes on to say:
By item 644 thereof wheat, wheat flour, semolina, and other wheat products, shall be entered free of duty from countries which do not impose a duty on wheat or wheat flour or semolina imported from the United States; otherwise the duty upon wheat is fixed at ten cents per bushel, and upon wheat flour at forty-five cents per barrel, and upon semolina and other products of wheat ten per centum ad valorem.
Read that again, to make sure that you are quoting the United States tariff.

I will read it again, because it seems hardly possible that the Minister of Finance should quote the United States tariff. The Minister of Finance actually ppints out to His Excellency the Governor General, that the United States has made a statutory offer to this Govemmeht to admit wheat, wheat flour, semolina and other wheat products into the United States free of duty if the Canadian people through their executive authority or their Parliament will place them on the free list. Is there any negotiation there? None, my hon. friend says. Is it not this, that when this legislation has gone into effect under the authority of the Order in Council, the admission of the products of the one country into the other is dependent upon the reciprocal legislation which these two countries have passed? How different is that from the arrangement of 1911, except as to the number pf articles which were to he admitted under reciprocal legislation?
It is the same thing.

These hon. gentlemen have said that they want no entangling alliances with the country to the south of us. In 1911 it was agreed that there should be no entangling alliances; it was agreed that each Parliament should be free and independent to legislate at any time to alter the duty in any way that might be thought in the best interest of its people. So, today, this Parliament is free; so to-day the Congress of the United States is free. Both cases are exactly similar. As I have said, there is not the slightest difference except as to the number of articles which were in the reciprocal arrangement of 1911 and the number in the reciprocal arrangement which you have to-day. What did my hon. friend do? Did he have no truck or trade with the Yankees? Did he not, the moment this Order in Council was passed, send a copy of it to the United States consul, so that he could inform the authorities at Washington that Canada would allow wheat, wheat flour and semolina to enter the United States free of duty? Then the Order in Council says:-
And whereas, if Canada should place wheat, wheat flour and semolina on the free list, our wheat and wheat products would gain free entry to the markets of the United States.
For the last six years you have said that Canada is going to legislate in her own interest; that Canada is to have no truck or trade with the Yankees that Canada is not going to base her fiscal policy on that of the United States. It is, however, pu't forward to His Excellency as a reason for placing these articles on the free list, not that that is to be of any advantage to the Canadian people, but that thereby we will get free entry into the great American market for the wheat and wheat products. Then the Order in Council says:-
And whereas it is desirable, in the national interest that, for the reasons stated above, free access should be obtained to the markets of the United States for Canada's wheat.
Not for Canada's low grade of wheat, not for this wheat that it is said we cannot sell to anybody else, but for Canada's wheat, her Manitoba hard, everything, all kinds of wheat. This Order in Council says, under the guiding hand of him who was once a strong Liberal, under the teachings which he had, in years gone by, when he was taught to believe it was desirable that Canadians should be given access to all the markets possible, and that there should be the greatest freedom possible in trading between these two great countries-under the guidance of the Minister of Finance, he-

cause it is ihe that makes this report, not the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Acting Premier-
Not the Solicitor General.

No, it is not the Solicitor General, but the Minister of Finance, who says:-
And whereas it is desirable in the national interest that, for the reasons stated above, free access should he obtained to the markets of the United States for Canada's wheat. Therefore, His Excellency the Governor General in Council, under the authority of the War Measures Act, 1914, section 6-
This temporary section, which expires when the war ends.
.-is pleased to order and it is hereby ordered that wheat, wheat flour and semolina be transferred to the list of goods which may be imported into Canada free of duty or customs.
The minister says that this is desirable in the national interests for reasons stated above. In view of the allegation that it is, as we on this side say that it was, that it has been for the last six years, and that it always has been, in the national interest that there should be a free exchange of wheat and wheat products between these two countries, what are the reasons that' animate this Government in advising His Excellency that Canadian wheat should have free -access to the United States? One is that a large amount of tonnage of wheat goes to the United States for shipment to Europe. I do not see that that would be any reason, because wheat could go into the United States under the law as it was before this Order in Council was passed, simply on the payment of the customs duty for bond, I think, of about one cent a bushel, or it may be even less than that. I have here a communication from the Secretary of the Board of Trade at Quebec. This is a public document, copies of which have probably been sent to other members of Parliament. It is dated the 14th of April, and says:
I would draw your attention to the following questions specially dealt with in this report:
1. The alarming- diversion of the grain trade of the Canadian Northwest to the United States ports. Notwithstanding the sacrifices made by Canada in building three transcontinental railways, 181 million bushels of our grain went to New York and other United States ports for shipment in 1916, as against 131 million bushels to points in Canada, for consumption as well as for export, of -which 40 million bushels subsequently went to Portland.
If the Quebec Board of Trade is right, then 221,000,000 bushels of Canadian grain

during the last year went through the United States to United -States ports, as against 91,000,000 bushels that went to points in Canada for consumption as well as' for export. Yet this is one of the actual conditions existing at this time which have induced the Minister of Finance to tell to His Excellency that it would be in the national interest that all restrictions should be taken away from the importation of wheat into the United States. Another circumstance is that the lower grade wheat cannot be marketed in Canada, and vast quantities of it-and that would seem to be borne out by the report of the Board of Trade-are marketed in the United States, notwithstanding the duty of ten cents per bushel, and-and this is one of the important and convincing circumstances-as at the present time the Canadian farmer is only able to sell under present circumstances his first class wheat at $2.29 per bushel, and is obliged to pay a duty of ten cents a bushel on even inferior grades of wheat imported into the United States, as he is to-day selling vast quantities of wheat in the United States and paying the duty, and as it is desirable to supply all the goods possible to the United Kingdom and her Allies, of which the United States is one-under these circumstances and in the national interest it is desirable to waive the duty and -so to secure these wheat -and wheat products shall go into the United States free. Have I not given the circumstances just as they are divulged by the Order in Council? If there are any other reasons to be given, tell me what they are. The Solicitor General, in one part of his speech, dwelt upon this fact, that it was desirable to send all the Canadian wheat possible through United States ports so that it would get to the Allies.
The fact that last year this vast quantity of Canadian wheat went into the United States would seem to destroy the argument which the solicitor submitted in that particular. No, Sir, the only justifiable ground upon which it can be put at all, is that this provision ought to be of a permanent character; that in times of war and in times of peace, so far as food products are concerned the tariff wall between the two countries should be torn down and the producers allowed to secure the best markets wherever they can in either one country or the other and the consumers buy at the lowest possible price. In setting forth their reasons hon. gentlemen opposite are deceiving themselves, and they think they can pull

the wool over the eyes of the people of this country, but they will not be able to do it. They have done what they have done, because they have not been able to stand up against the strong expression of opinion from the farmers of the North West. My hon. friend stated at Valleyfield, that in 1911, when he was only thirty years of age, and his mind was not fully developed, he had opposed a local navy. There is a feeling in this House and in the country that the reason this Government returned the tenders and refused to give a contract for the construction of ten war vessels-cruisers and destroyers-under the Naval Act of 1909, was the pledge which the Minister of Inland Revenue and his associates had exacted that there should be no Canadian navy. Now, after a lapse of

six years, and when his mind has presumably, as he himself says, developed far beyond what it was when he was thirty, he regrets his conduct at that time in opposing a local navy. Let me appeal to him to say to his colleagues, with all the influence which he ought to be able to command as coming from the great province of Quebec, so wealthy and With such a large population, that the time has come when the Government of Canada might well follow the example of Great Britain and the United States and engage with all its resources and all its energies in the building of ships. If he does this he will not only si ow that he regrets his action in 1911, but be will take the most effective measures to undo the harm done by the pledge which he and his associates exacted from the Conservative party at the elections of 1911. In view of the difficulty which England and her Allies are experiencing in getting foodstuffs, in view of the appeals made by Mr. Balfour to the United States, to send whatever ships they can, whether wooden ' vessels, cruisers, destroyers, or even tug boats,
I say that the greatest crime that any government ever committed against the people was the deliberate determination on the part of this Government not to build ships in Canada. We have lost five or six years, during which great results' could have been obtained.
And we have lost prestige.

And we have lost prestige. Incalculable harm has been done to the Empire and to Canada. Let me implore my hon. friend to declare at an end the promise which he is alleged and believed to have exacted from the Prime Minister in 1911 j let him declare that the past is forgotten and that we must, even at this late date, begin to do our duty to Canada and the Empire by engaging in the building of ships, not war ships -alone, but also commercial vessels.

Before I conclude, Mr. Speaker, let me cftl your attention for a few minutes to this amendment proposed by my hon. friend (Mr. Turriff) and which my hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) says is wholly political in its character. I would have thought, had it not been for the remarks of the Solicitor General, that it was one of the most-inoffensive amendments that was ever presented in this House of Commons by a member of the Opposition. I think they ought to accept it.

One would think so. My hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) says that it was not intended as a party resolution at all. It is not intended as a vote of want of confidence.
