I am authorized by the acting leader of this side of the House to-night to say that the gentlemen who will be called upon, and who will cheerfully, we hope, vote for this resolution, will not be doing it as expressing any want of confidence in the Government in the ordinary -sense. Therefore, if they can support this resolution, they can support it in perfect confidence that it will only express what this House ought to express and that no immediate harm can bo done to the Government because we must wait until the people have an opportunity of exercising their judgment -in reference to their conduct. Let me read it and see just what it says:
That all the words after the word "that" be struck out and' the following substituted therefor.
The hon. gentleman says that it contains a great laudation of the Opposition. It does not. It says:
This House desires -to take the earliest opportunity of expressing its pleasure that the Government has at last yielded to the persistent demands of the Grain Growers of the West as frequently set forth by delegations and resolutions of the representatives of the farming interest, and repeatedly voiced by the Liberal party in this House, by placing wheat, wheat flour and semolina on the free list, and thereby securing a free market for wheat and wheat products in the United States.



Is not every word of that true? Is there any objection to be taken to our expressing our gratification that this has been done? We do not take a childish view of this order. We do not want to gain any political kudos from it. We might seek to embarrass the Government, but what we say in effect is that we as members of the Liberal party in this House and in this country have been for years demanding, in the national interest, that wheat and its products be placed on the free list, we have been calling attention to the opportunities for vast growth, development and increased prosperity in our western country if this were done, and we have been urging that it should be done in the interest of Canada. Well, now, should the Government object to our expressing our gratification that they have at last yielded to our demands and the demands of the people of the West and passed this order? The Solicitor General himself has said that everything here is true, because he says in effect that the western farmers kept agitating and agitating, and that the Liberal party helped them during all these years, that the Liberal party egged them on and encouraged them until it got to be so infernally hot that the Tory Government could no longer resist the demand made upon them. Is not that in effect what the Solicitor General said? Why should we not express pleasure that the Government have at last acted upon our suggestion and placed wheat on the free list? That is all we ask you gentlemen to do. Are you not gratified that you have done it? 1 beg your pardon, Mr. Speaker, may I ask, through you, Sir, if they are not gratified that they have done it? We are accustomed to see their smiling faces, but, looking at them this afternoon and seeing how glum and solemn they looked while the Solicitor General was giving utterance to his very eloquent, but, it seemed to me, laboriously conceived speech, it indicated that perhaps they were not so gratified as the Government would like to think them to be. But pretend to be; let me appeal to them to look as if they were gratified, to join with us on this side of the House and as a unanimous Parliament, representing the people of this country, let us declare that we are all gratified that at last this great measure of trade freedom has been passed into law, and that hereafter the farmers	of our western country can

towards the realization of Canada's destiny

rectly opposed to this resolution. But it does seem to me that it is absolutely necessary to make this policy permanent in order that it shall have that beneficial effect that we desire that it should have. In our western *country, out of perhaps one hundred million acres or perhaps two hundred million acres of arable land, we have only about twenty million acres under cultivation. We want to encourage settlers to come in from the United States. They form perhaps the best settlers who can be brought into that country. I know one section of our Northwest where up to 1900 or 1902 there was scarcely any settlement at all. There had been a railroad running through that section for six years, but for sixty or seventy miles there was not a settler upon that line. About 1902 American settlers began to come across. They had experts analyze the soil, they undertook the cultivation of the land, and in that section of the country to-day vast areas are sown with wheat, and it is among the very garden spots of the Dominion of Canada., Americans make splendid settlers. Now, if you can show to these people that it is the permanent policy of the people of Canada to have free wheat, you will encourage people to come over from the United States, not by thousands but by hundreds of thousands, because they will look forward to farming in that country becoming very profitable indeed.
They know that' the large market of the United States is of enormous benefit to the farmer. They will be encouraged to come in, and our country will move ahead with very much greater rapidity and certainty. Leave the matter indefinite, leave it to have a temporary character, leave it so that the Government might tomorrow or three months from now or next fall even, when the war is over or before, cancel this Order, destroy the effect of this Order altogether and re-impose a duty on wheat and wheat products, and you m^ke the farmer timid, you make the settler timid and you will not achieve any important results either in the way of immigration or in the way of development of our country or advancement of prosperity.

Mr. FRANK S. SCOTT (South Waterloo): Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsiey) will pardon me if I do not attempt to follow him in the arguments which he has presented in his speech to-night.

In the Budget introduced a few days ago by the Minister of Finance there were no new principles, no new methods of taxation. In the Budget of 1915 a very radical change by way of tariff increase was made. I have noted, however, a very great difference between the way in which the Budget of 1917 has been received by 'hon. gentlemen opposite and their reception of the Budget of 1915. Hon. gentlemen opposite took very strong exception to the Budget of 1915 and the proposals that were therein made. So strong was their opposition to the Budget of that year that an amendment was introduced. One of their chief dbjec-tions was that it would not produce revenue. I have not heard any 'hon. gentleman opposite who has taken part in this debate argue that the present Budget, although there is no change in that respect, will not produce revenue. Another argument that was advanced two

years ago was that the Budget of 1915 would stifle trade. In the discussion that has taken place upon the Budget it has not been argued by hon. gentlemen opposite that the present proposals of the Finance Minister will stifle trade. We know that since 1915 the trade of Canada has been more buoyant than it ever was before. We were told in 1915 that the tariff proposals of that day would be a burden on the people; yet it has not been contended during the last few days by hon. gentlemen opposite that the tariff of to-day, which is identical with the tariff of 1915, would place any undue burden upon the people. The Budget of 1915 produced revenue without parallel in Canada's history. As to the so-called burdens that were imposed upon the people, thfi taxes were paid willingly and cheerfully, and there has been no undue hardship. In the light of our experience during the past few years, the Minister of Finance can take a great deal of encouragement from his recommendations of 1915, and can look forward with confidence to the future.
Since the bringing down of the Budget a few days ago, another line of argument has been followed by hon. gentlemen opposite. They claim that a sufficient share of the burden of the war is not being borne by the people of to-day; that we are leaving too much to posterity. The words of the chief financial critic of the Opposition were:-
Are we now doing- our full duty, or are we leaving too much to the future to pay? I believe that we are borrowing too much and paying too little.
What are the facts? We were told by the Finance Minister the other day that after paying all expenses for one year and providing for capital expenditure, out of the revenue of this Dominion there still remained a surplus of $60,000,000 to be applied to the carrying on of the war. Included in the ordinary expenditure was $25,000,000 interest upon war expenditure and for pensions. We were told by the member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames) the other day that the Canadian public have contributed to the Patriotic Fund, Red Cross and other patriotic organizations the annual sum of $15,000,000 or $20,000,000. Taking the surplus of $60,000,000, the amount of $25,000,000 that has been paid for interest on war debt and for pensions, and the amount at least of $15,000,000 that has been subscribed voluntarily by the Canadian people for patriotic purposes, you have a total of $100,000,000. In 1912 the
total revenue of Canada was $135,000,000, and in 1914, $175,000,000. The people of Canada during the last year have contributed directly toward the carrying on of the war a total of $100,000,000, 73 per cent of the total revenue in 1912 or 57 per cent of the total revenue in 1914.
In every country it has always been a difficult question and one which has given rise to much difference of opinion, to decide what proportion of the cost of war should be paid out of current revenue and what proportion should be obtained by borrowing. I think that financial people, the world over, will agree that for a country like Canada so to re-arrange her financial affairs as to be able to make a contribution of this kind directly towards the "war, is certainly a splendid record. As this debate has proceeded, there has been perhaps too much of a tendency, one perhaps not confined alone to this House, but a tendency that has been somewhat general throughout the country, to deprecate, to belittle what the Dominion of Canada has-done in connection with this war. It is right, of course, that we should keep spurred on, as it were, that we should do all possible in connection with the war; but, from a national standpoint, it seems to me we would make a mistake if we tried to minimize what we have accomplished. It is a good thing for a man sometimes to get an outside view of his own business, and as it is with individuals, may it not be so with a nation? If, as Canadians, we could come in contact with the people of the neighbouring republic to the south, visit the cities of New York and Boston, meet there the average American citizen and hear what he has to say, hear the estimate which he has placed upon what Canada has done in this war, we would have a different idea, and a greater satisfaction than we ever had before, of the appreciation in which we are held by outside observers.
I do hot intend to say anything upon the question of free wheat, because that has been so fully dealt with by other speakers. There was, however, one criticism that was made by the hon.- member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) in connection with the action of the Government on this matter of free wheat, and it seemed to me that his point was not well taken. His argument was that the Government of to-day had adopted a policy of free wheat. He went further than some of the other critics of the Opposition in that he very

warmly commended the Government for it ; but his criticism was this, that while the Government had adopted this policy, it should have adopted it two years ago, and that great disadvantage had accrued to Canada. His argument was that countries like Sweden, Germany, Austria and other countries, immediately after the outbreak of war, had taken the same action; that they had removed the duties from foodstuffs, and that they had given their people this advantage. As I have understood all this agitation for free wheat, the arguments that have been advanced by hon. gentlemen opposite, and the position taken by t'he grain growers of the West, their standpoint was. not that it would reduce the price of wheat in the Dominion of Canada, hut rather that it would enable them to get a higher price for it in the American market. In my view, an argument or criticism of that kind is quite unjustifiable and illogical. The hon. member for Red Deer also said that the world had learned many lessons as a result of this war. There can he no doubt of that, and that things in general, in Canada and in every other country in the world, will be changed vastly as a result of this war; but the deduction which he drew was that, as a result of this war, the Dominion of Canada, having regard for what free trade Britain had been able to do, her splendid record of achievement, would be well advised to adopt a policy of freedom of trade as they have had it in Great Britain for so many years. He compared Britain's present record with that of Germany. As I said a moment ago. there are many lessons to be learned from this war, tout the lesson that Canada should learn from it is directly opposite to the lesson which the hon. member from Red Deer would attempt to apply to Canada. Compare Germany and Russia. This war has demonstrated 'beyond any possible doubt that no agricultural nation can withstand a war with an industrial nation. Forty years ago Britain was unrivalled as an industrial nation; there was no comparison at all in an industrial sense between Great Britain and Germany. Forty years ago Germany adopted a policy of protection, and under it her industries developed until she became Great Britain's most powerful competitor in all the markets of the world. The comparison I want to draw' is this:	Russia is a land
of great natural resources; her soil is more fertile, and she has a greater population than Germany. Russia continued as she had been doing; she had m 
effect the conditions as described by the hon. member for Red Deer, namely, absolute freedom of trade. She depended upon agriculture; she bought her manufactured goods in the most convenient and cheapest markets. Yet, if the statesmen of Russia could live over the past forty years, is there any reasonable-minded man to-day, who, in view of the events which have occurred during the last two years, will believe that the statesmen of Russia would abide by a policy of that kind?
It was, I think, the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) who said that we could thank the Kaiser for the prosperous condition that had existed in Canada during the past two years. A statement of that kind is scarcely fair. We can thank the Kaiser for the war, but we can thank the Government, and the late Minister of Militia in particular, in very large measure, for the prosperity which has come to this Dominion, through the manufacture of munitions of war. I would say further than that, that the people of Canada to-day can thank not only the present Government that has founded this great munition work, and the Minister of Finance for the credit of hundreds of millions of dollars which he has established in Canada for the benefit of the British Government, but we must go farther back than. that. Almost forty years ago this Dominion of Canada embarked upon the National Policy of Protection, and I ask you, Sir, if the statesmen of Canada had not adopted that policy forty years ago, would Canada to-day he in a position to take the part she has taken in the war during the last two years. A great industrial fabric such as we have in Canada is of slow growth; it cannot be built up in a day, and it is fortunate indeed that when this war came on the Dominion of Canada had a well established system ,of industries that enabled us not only to provide munitions for the carrying on of the war, but to discharge our heavy financial obligations in a "way that we otherwise could not have done.
'The hpur is late and I do not intend to trespass further on the time of the House, but I wish to take this opportunity of congratulating the Minister of Finance on the splendid statement he has been able to present. From the experience which Canada has already had of the operation of the tariff as laid down in the budget .of 1915, and of the special methods of taxation which have been adopted, I am convinced that Canada will be able to carry on success-


fully 'the part she has ch-osen for herself in this war, and will win a high and creditable place for herself among the nations of the world in this great struggle.

The observations made by ordinary members of the House such as myself on an occasion such as this, when the Budget is being discussed, are in the way of a review of the record of the Government, or so much of it as is already written, and in the way pf an analysis of the policy of the Government so far as its future programme is disclosed. This duty which is cast upon a member, and, indeed, upon all sections of our people when they peruse a budget debate, is emphasized and intensified when the occasion is one such as this, when there is the probability of a general election before very long. I am not saying either yes or no to the question whether there should be a general election in the Dominion of Canada this year, but the fact remains that there is a great possibility, and even a probability, of one being held. In analysing the record of this Government one naturally examines it under two distinct heads: their administration during the times of peace, and their administration during the war. You cannot examine these two periods together for they are essentially and organically different, and a separate stewardship has to be rendered for each period. If before we have another Budget speech the people are asked whether this Government shall be continued in office, it will be their duty first and foremost to examine the two periods in a composite way. The first three years the Government were in office was a period during which ordinary normal conditions prevailed, that is to say, it was a time of peace as contrasted with war times. I am not going to dwell on the record of the Government during these three years other than to emphasize that in our perusal of their record during the war period we must not forget that just as much importance, if not more so, should be attached to an examination of their record during the days of peace, because the peace days, after all, are the days when normal conditions prevail.
Let us throw our minds back for a moment to those three years of peace when hon. gentlemen opposite were in power, and I think on that score the Government stand almost self-convicted. We are so engrossed in the war that we are sometimes apt to forget what a mighty deliverance it was to hqn. gentlemen opposite.
Before the war came they were in sore straits; desperation was written on their brow. They did not know whether to go to the country and dare the worst, or wait a few months longer, when conditions might be still more desperate. You will recall, Sir, that tragic and eventful summer and fall of 1914, when hon. gentlemen opposite bad almost got their courage screwed up to the point of taking the plunge, before things got more desperate. The record of the Government during those three years, I say, was one of failure, and we have every Teason to believe that the same policy will prevail and the same sort of administration be given in times of peace if hon. gentlemen opposite are returned to power.
Let me recall the condition of affairs in 1914. I do not know whether you live in a city or town, Mr. Speaker, but throughout Canada at that time there prevailed the greatest stagnation; there was a condition of poverty almost in many of our cities and towns. In my own city of Moosejaw, which before that day had always been prosperous, and where the bread-winner of the family never need worry, men walked the streets by the hundreds, if not by the thousands, unable to get work, earnestly as they desired it. Those are the facts, and those were the conditions that prevailed throughout the whole Dominion of Canada. They had said, Let well enough alone; do not encourage the farmer by giving him reciprocity; we will have no truck and-trade with the Yankees; and the result was the unfortunate conditions of affairs that we saw throughout the whole Dominion of Canada. At the time these men were walking the streets of our cities looking for work, what did we see in our great agricultural districts? Great zones of land were calling for men to till them, simply crying out for labour, and although there were thousands of men walking the streets of our cities and towns, the two were never brought together. The secret of the development and prosperity of Canada during the fifteen years the Laurier Government was in power was that conditions on the land were made inviting to labour, and the men responded to the call of the soil, and made possible the great development of this Dominion. And if on that occasion reciprocity had been adopted, if encouragement had been given to the husbandmen by the opening of markets, ithe lowering of tariffs and the making of conditions more inviting, we have every reason to believe, the Dominion of Canada would have continued after 1911

the prosperity that it had experienced for fifteen years before that time. But these hon. gentlemen decided that they had a chance to demonstrate the success or failure of their policy, and they most successfully demonstrated the failure of it. So, I say, the question we shall have to ask ourselves is, whether or not it will be wise for the people to continue the Government in power. We have the experience of three years at least to test them by, and they are very important years to enable us to estimate the profitableness or the reverse of the administration they have given and the policy they have carried into effect. We have had three years of war. All that is fresh in our minds, three sad, ibloody years of war. And we have seen sights that have made us ashamed day and night. We have seen men lining their pockets, we have seen men doing things such as those for which, even in Austria, men are lined up against a stone wall and shot-that is, taking advantage of their country's dire distress for their own gain. For things not so bad as we have seen here, men in Manchester, as I read in one account, were *sent to penitentiary for five years-men who had some patronage to give and who accepted gifts, though not a word was said about bribing them. We have made such men honorary colonels or have given them other honours. But, as I say, when we come to ascertain whether this Administration is worthy of our confidence because of its record in the war years, we shall have to consider two things if nothing more -the Boss rifle, and the case of John Wesley Allison. These are enough, in my opinion, to drive ten governments out of power. I do not lay these things at the door of the late Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Sam Hughes) but I lay them at the door of the Prime Minister (Sir Bobert Borden). He was warned-I heard him warned in this Chamber and in the old House, again and again over a period of eighteen months -'that he was putting into the soldier's hands a weapon that was useless. But for some reason, I will not say what the reason was, the lives of our soldiers were counted as nothing against the desire to *continue the Boss rifle.

Does the hon. gentleman know that the Liberal press of Quebec, French and English, have published strong protests against this Government because they had ceased to manufacture Boss rifles in the factory?

because he could not wait seventy-two hours to make this change constitutionally, but rushed it through by an Order in Council under the War Measures Act. If, a year ago, this was an outrageous thing to do, it is hard to take the minister seriously when he says that it was urgent, immediate^ pressing, that the Government could not wait until Parliament met seventy-two hours afterwards. No sooner is it done than the same afternoon it is hustled off to Mr. Foster, the representative of the Yankees, and wired into Washington, in order that they might have it in force if possible next morning at ten o'clock when the customs offices opened. Talk about truck and trade with the Yankees; if the hon. gentleman experienced a conversion, it came to him with terrible suddenness, it came to him like a bolt, because he could not wait until the House met when the matter might have been attended to by Parliament.
He might have lost the inspiration.

We would like him to make it permanent lest he get another inspiration and take it away from us just as suddenly. The views of the hon. Minister of Public Works were along the same lines. The minister used these words, Hansard, 1916, page 884. He says that Canadian wheat has such a high name that it would be wrong to detract from that high standard, and he goes on:
The fact is that Canadian wheat commands a price at the American seaboard of from twenty to twenty-five cents a bushel more than the American wheat. That is one of the reasons why I say this House would fail in its duty to the farming- community of Western Canada if it did not reject the resolution of my hon. friend.
And the same hon gentleman a few days later spoke along similar lines, Hansard, 1916, page 1049:
"We have to-day a position of great advantage with our wheat, a position which we have won gradually by our own efforts. Beyond question of doubt all these conditions justify us, having in view the interests of the farmers themselves, in rejecting this resolution, and thereby permitting these favourable conditions to continue.
His view was that if that resolution was adopted those favourable conditions would be taken away and a serious wrong would be done to the people of the West. At page 1050 he said:
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it is our plain duty, having in regard the best interests of the Canadian farming community, to adhere to

our good old traditional policy of keeping Canada for the Canadians.
And he goes on at page 1051 and says:-
I say that we should appreciate the advantage of our position and that we would fail in our duty, especially to the farming community of Canada, and more especially of Western Canada, if we did not rejeot the resolution of my hon. friend for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff), in which he proposes to divert our wheat into American channels as much as possible and thereby allow, it to be mixed with American wheat, in which case we would have to go over again all the work that we have done in the past to establish our own transcendent identity in the markets of the world.
Similarly, the hon. Solicitor 'General expressed himself on different pages, for instance pages 1071 and 1073; I shall not take the time to read what he said. But one thing he said was that of the desire for free wheat. 90 per cent was politics and 10 per cent falsehood, and now he is going to give us the whole 100 per cent for no other reason than that he may get a little peace. So, I wish to emphasize the point that we are driven to the conclusion that the Government are not sincere in dealing with the question on its merits. It is remarkable that a Government, elected to power as that Government was, should come out plainly and flatly and announce a change of view on this question of the tariff and of trading with the Yankees. We should know where we are. We are not content with a mere bone thrown to us while they still deny the underlying principle which is the subject of division between the two parties. Hon. gentlemen opposite would like to make it appear that there is nothing between the Liberals and the Conservatives. That is their stock argument especially in the West. I would say frankly that I regret there is not more difference between them, hut there is enough difference between them to make it clear that the Liberal party is the one we should support. The Liberal party favours a lowfer tariff and open markets, and these are grand British doctrines. I believe that the hon. the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Burrell), with his knowledge of agriculture, will agree that an open market is	not a bad thing
for a farmer who has things to sell. And so I say there is that cleavage between the two parties. But we in the West are not satisfied with what has been given to us. Do not let any one suppose that we are. We are not content with this moiety that is given to us, much less than a moiety. We want the rights that are ours. We want the open market in all things we

have to sell, above all things in our flax. We raise great quantities of flax. Hon gentlemen opposite said in 1911 that if we sold our flax to the Americans, which we did in any event and paid twenty-five cents a bushel duty on it, into the treasury of the United States we remained loyal Britishers; but if we got our flax into the United States without paying twenty-five cents a bushel to Uncle Sam's treasury our British blood would all go away with our flax and we would become Yankees. By what reasoning we know not, they tried to get away with this kind of argument, and did largely get away with it in Ontario. We are not content, we want free flax into the United States. Our flax goes there anyway, and it is simply a matter of en-r:ching the American treasury. We want free trade in fruit and many things that are denied to us which we would have secured under reciprocity. Let me say that whatever the policy of the Liberal party may be, and I am not high enough up m it to give a lecture on that policy, my policy is everything free that you can get free and a great many more things than were free under Liberals or Conservatives. Our own side were in power for fifteen years. I have said and repeat that my mind is clear as to which party it is my duty in the interest of my constituents to support. But my mind is just as clear in saying that neither party is anywhere near what I should like to see. Both parties, I think, have too many Conservatives in them, whether you call them Liberals or Conservatives. There are too many Conservative-Liberals in our party to suit me. I wish that a committee of western Canadians could be allowed to nominate all candidates for the Liberal party in the next election. That would ensure the selection of true Liberals; there would be no reactionaries in the party, but as the Liberal party ought to do, it would come out frankly and say what its policy was. There are forty-two seats and will be forty-two candidates in the Prairie Provinces, and I have counselled-and I hope it will be done-that the forty-two candidates of the Liberal party should act as one unit and have their arrangements to act as a unit before the election, and then they will come down here with the power they ought to have. I am not for separating from the rest of Canada, as yet certainly. So far as the money goes, we are paying all right for our connection with
Canada. There is no protection to us. We are paying for protection at every turn we make, and it is a terrible burden on our poor homesteaders, and there are many of them in my own riding. There have been more homesteaders come into my riding than into any other two ridings in the West during the ten years I have been a member. Therefore I say that the western members in the future should lay down a policy to act as one unit, and if they cannot make the two parties sit up and take notice it will be a strange thing. We have the numbers now and we are going to have them. I think it time the people in this House understood) that the people of western Canada are not tied up to either party eternally, but they are tied up with the principle of low tariff and open markets, and for my part, whether I should be a member of the next House or not-and I do not expect I shall because I do not expect to be a candidate-I believe the time has come when the Dominion of Canada should realize that the best prosperity of the whole Dominion is synonymous and parallel with the prosperity of western Canada. Which has made the whole of Canada prosperous to-day is that the late Laurier Government adopted a policy which made conditions so attractive in our great undeveloped prairies that people went in by hundreds of thousands, and having gone in they devel- -oped the country and made national wealth; and it is by a resumption and restoration of that policy and further development of it that the same good, prosperous conditions will be restored to the Dominion of Canada.
We want freedom of foodstuffs, freedom of fruit, freedom of lumber, of agricultural implements, and we want all the open markets of the world which we can get. If one party will not get those advantages for us it is time we made a party in the West and gave the people to understand that we are really in earnest in our desire to get what we believe to be justice in these matters.
We believe that justice was denied us in 1911. We believe that a political trick was played on the people of Canada, in Ontario by making one cry, in Quebec by making another. A false, spurious un-British cry was made there, one that was a disgrace to the whole Dominion of Canada. But it turned the trick for the time being. But the people of the West are not the kind to give up on one election, and they will continue to fight. Even if they have free wheat temporarily, they are not satisfied with it but are determined to keep up the

struggle to the end that they may receive justice at the hands of the whole Parliament of Canada, from which legislation must come. They are not secessionists, but their belief is that the prosperity of the Dominion of Canada will be found to be synonymous with the prosperity of western Canada.
Nothing can be more sane and reasonable than the resolution before the House; and if our friends opposite will not even agree to remove the doubt, and there certainly is a doubt, it seems to me that they are not desirous of meeting us half way. It seems to me beyond question that it is the purpose of the Government, according to their plausible statement, to give free wheat, and, if so, why not set the matter beyond peradventure and agree to this resolution in the House when it comes to a vote. I regret that I shall not be able to be here for the vote. I hope, however, that hon. gentlemen opposite will then have reconsidered this matter, and that they will show a united front with us in agreeing to this resolution and making it unanimous.
On motion of Mr. Barnard the debate was adjourned.
